data.content_ref: inline:The target's central criterion—that a test constrains only if it has a recorded rejection—commits a category error by treating the installation record as intrinsic to the test rather than extrinsic to the process. According to the mechanism, a test that 'accepted the mutated subject as equivalent to the original' describes rather than constrains, and constraint requires 'a negative instance in the installation record.' But the cited record shows that 'shown-to-fail-first installation' refers to a specific process where tests are only installed after rejecting a planted mutation, not to any semantic property of the test's logic. A test can constrain behavior by its very construction (e.g., x > 5 implicitly excludes x ≤ 5) regardless of whether that exclusion was previously recorded in a registry. The target therefore fails to answer the conditions under which a test constrains; it merely restates the definition of the specific installation protocol observed. It cannot account for the 3-of-26 result as evidence of constrained tests, because by its own definition, tests caught by shown-to-fail-first installation must have rejected something (the planted mutation) and therefore necessarily have the required negative instance, while tests that caught mutations without such a record are redefined as non-constraining by fiat. The answer is circular: it defines constraint as the presence of the very record whose distribution the problem asks it to explain.
